title: Shishupala
hook: a light rises from the fallen king and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira finishes his rite
carry: where you'd rather turn that light

segments.voice: Yesterday Shishupala's hundred pardons ran out, and Krishna spoke to the kings before he acted. Name your limit, kindly and clearly.
screen: `PATIENCE WITH A SHAPE AND A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Shishupala has fallen, and the hall is silent. But the poem isn't done with him. Something rises from his body: a radiance, the text says, bright as the sun. Every eye in the hall follows it. It moves toward Krishna, bows to him, and enters him. The man who railed against Krishna in front of every king ends inside him. It's a strange ending, and the poem says the kings who saw it were amazed.
screen: `A LIGHT RISES FROM HIS BODY.` → `IT BOWS TO KRISHNA.` → `IT ENTERS HIM.`

segments.voice: What does it mean that Shishupala's light enters Krishna? The poem shows it and moves on, so readers have filled the space. Some Hindus, especially in devotional traditions, read it this way: Shishupala thought about Krishna constantly, even if every thought was hatred, and that fierce, single-minded attention brought him to Krishna in the end. Others read it more simply: everything that lives returns, at last, to its source. The text doesn't settle it, and i won't either. Then the story turns practical. Yudhishthira, the host, has the funeral rites performed for Shishupala, and places Shishupala's son on the throne of Chedi. The fallen king's line keeps its crown. The rite is finished, the guests are honored and sent home, and Krishna returns to his own city. Look back at the week. The Rajasuya, with everyone handed a job: Krishna washing feet, Duryodhana receiving the gifts. Bhishma named Krishna for the first honor, and Shishupala stood up. He made his case, and Yudhishthira answered with gentleness. The kings grew angry; Bhishma spoke of a sleeping lion, and held Bhima back. Then the cradle and a promise of a hundred pardons, the limit and the discus, and now the light. Shishupala's story ends here. But remember the cousin at the gift table. He's still in Indraprastha, and the next story is his.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE LIGHT MEAN?` · `THE FUNERAL, AND A NEW KING.` · `THE RITE IS FINISHED.` · `LOOKING BACK AT THE WEEK.` · then, large: `THE COUSIN AT THE GIFT TABLE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've had real trouble with, someone who takes up a lot of room in your thoughts. You don't have to change how you feel; just see your attention as a light you've been shining at them, and with each slow breath, gather a little of it back home. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer for a moment; if not, simply let your attention rest.
Shishupala. Krishna's cousin and fierce opponent, pardoned a hundred times, whose light rose at the end and entered Krishna.
Your line: where you'd rather turn that light. Tomorrow, a hall that plays tricks. That's the week.

howItsDone: In some devotional traditions, the end of Shishupala is told as a teaching that even hatred, if it fixes the mind on Krishna, can bring a person to him; other readers take a different meaning, and the Mahabharata itself does not explain the light.

fork.setup: you're one of the kings in the hall. Shishupala has fallen, and a light rises from his body. where does it go?
fork.reveal: the poem says the light bowed to Krishna and entered him, and the kings were amazed. it shows this without explaining it.

original.note: Sanskrit tejas: radiance, brilliant energy; a light like this rises from Shishupala and enters Krishna.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story ends when Shishupala dies.
what it means: a light rises from him and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira gives him a funeral and crowns his son.
what a scholar hears: the text shows the light without explaining it, and later devotional readers took it as a teaching about the power of a mind fixed on Krishna.
recall: kept watch while his family slept

chat.says: What happened to Shishupala's kingdom after he died at the ceremony?
options: Yudhishthira held his funeral rites and put Shishupala's son on the throne of Chedi.
Krishna took over the kingdom of Chedi and ruled it from his own city.
Yudhishthira added Chedi to his own lands as part of the Rajasuya.
chat.meaning: Yudhishthira, as a just host, had the funeral rites performed and placed Shishupala's son on the throne. The line kept its crown.

Indraprastha.meaning: the Pandavas' city, where the Rajasuya is held

Rajasuya.meaning: a royal consecration where kings honor one sovereign

Duryodhana.meaning: eldest of the Kaurava cousins, rival of the Pandavas

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sisupala-badha Parva (the radiance rising from Shishupala's body and entering Krishna; funeral rites; Shishupala's son installed; the Rajasuya completed)
Bhagavata Purana, Book 7, chapter 1 (the teaching that fixing the mind on the Lord, even in enmity, leads to him, with Shishupala as an example)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the radiance rising from Shishupala's body, bowing to Krishna and entering him, and the kings' amazement.
